https://www.dw.com/en/how-germany-s-dron.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5IlIk One defense method: Interceptor drones chase drones and capture them with a net Image: Sina Schuldt/dpa/picture alliance Advertisement How could a drone laden with explosives fly unhindered into Leipzig/Halle airport, where it remained apparently unnoticed for several hours? After last week's incident, German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt spoke of a "hybrid attack scenario" which he suspected came from "foreign powers." Suspicion has been directed at Russia, also because the drone was said to have been located near a Ukrainian Antonov cargo plane. The Federal Prosecutor's Office has taken over the investigation. The fact that the drone was loaded with explosives and able to reach the airport demonstrates a new level of threat. However, drone sightings over airports and ports, industrial sites and military properties have been increasing in Germany. In 2025, Germany's Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA) recorded more than 1,000 suspicious drone flights . Last October, drones disrupted air traffic in Munich for several hours, stranding numerous passengers. There is not sufficient drone protection at German airports, warned security expert Nico Lange. "We do not possess the sensor networks and sensor beams needed to spot all types of drones, especially low-flying, slow drones," he told DW. Leipzig drone threat prompts security concerns in Germany To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video The European Association for Unmanned Aviation has also long pointed out weak points in Germany's drone defense. "That a drone could apparently reach the airport tarmac and be discovered rather by chance, shows where the core of the problem is," said chairperson Gerald Wissel in relation to the latest incident. The association suggests "the establishment of real-time monitoring of the lower airspace as well as the mandatory tracking of all airspace participants via ADS-L" — a radio communications system that makes drones in an airspace electronically visible. State police, federal police, or Bundeswehr For a long time, Germany did little to address the issue of drone defense. Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt wants to remedy this by setting up new institutions. In December, he launched the Joint Counter Drone Center (GDAZ) in Berlin. There, information from the federal police, state police, secret service and armed forces is collated around the clock. But the incident at Leipzig airport shows that even a new hub is of little use if a dangerous drone at a large airport cannot be discovered and intercepted. Drones move quickly. Responses must therefore be decided within minutes. Doing so is made more difficult by Germany's system of divided responsibilities. If a suspicious drone takes off, it is initially a matter for the state police. Germany has 16 police authorities, one for each of its 16 states. It is only when the drone moves over a large airport or railway facility that the federal police are allowed to step in. Europe's defense: Latest drone technology shown in Berlin To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Unclear responsibilities Security experts and opposition politicians in Germany's Bundestag federal parliament have called for clear regulation and consolidation of responsibilities. "The muddle over responsibilities in drone defense is a substantial danger to our domestic security," said Irene Mihalic, lawmaker with the opposition Green Party and herself a former police officer. Many, including the Greens, suggest that the federal police should take the lead when it comes to drone defense. In December 2025, the federal police set up a new special unit for drone defense. Following the incident at Leipzig airport, Interior Minister Dobrindt wants to expand this. Originally, 130 staff positions across 4 locations were planned. In the future, there will be 300 personnel across 8 locations, to "be on site quickly and flexibly when needed," according to the Interior Ministry. Who is allowed to shoot down a drone in Germany? As so often happens following dramatic incidents, there have also been calls to use the Bundeswehr , Germany's armed forces. Many suggested that the military should be deployed for drone defense efforts at airports. However, current German law maintains that the police are responsible for upholding security within the country. A defense ministry spokesperson warned that protecting its own facilities, with their "tens of thousands of kilometers of fencing" is already a challenge for the Bundeswehr. Adding 24/7 protection of civilian infrastructure "would proclaim a false sense of security that we could never achieve," he argued. In an emergency, the police are allowed to ask the army for assistance. To achieve legal clarity in this regard, Germany amended its air security law in March. For the first time, it allows the Bundeswehr to shoot down drones outside their own premises to prevent "a particularly serious disaster." From printing to presses to drones To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Airports and train stations still lack protection There is also lot of catching up to do when it comes to the technical equipment for defending against drones. "There were big announcements at airports about positioning drone defense systems. They are more like detection systems. So far, they have not intercepted a single drone and at some airports they have still not yet been put in place," Manuel Atug, a spokesperson for the independent Critical Infrastructure Working Group (Arbeitsgruppe Kritische Infrastruktur) told DW. The German Police Union (GdP) is also lamenting the lack of resources for drone defense. "Unsafe train stations, unsafe airports and a police force which has to beg for money, law changes and the latest defense technology are really disconcerting," criticized GdP federal chairman Jochen Kopelke. A spokesperson for the German Interior Ministry advised that the large airports were steadily being equipped with drone defense technology. "The federal police have already procured a considerable amount of equipment. The 8 large airports are prioritized: Frankfurt (Main), Munich, Berlin, Düsseldorf, Hamburg, Cologne/Bonn, Stuttgart and Leipzig/Halle." The plan is for all of these airports to be equipped with mobile drone defense technology by the end of this year. This article was originally written in German. https://www.politico.eu/article/trump-eu.text: WARSAW — Ukraine has more leverage than a year ago — and European leaders are warning Donald Trump not to squander it by pressuring Kyiv to ease up on Russia. "In less than two years we went from the stage of no cards to the stage of don't play your cards," Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha told an audience at the Warsaw Security Conference. "That's a true achievement." Last year, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy was ambushed in the Oval Office by Trump, who ridiculed him for having "no cards" to play against Russia. Advertisement Advertisement Trump’s recent demand that Zelenskyy “better damn well stop” Ukraine’s refinery attacks, and his call for Ukraine to install a new leader, amount to a recognition that Kyiv does indeed have significant leverage in the fight. Kyiv’s refinery campaign is helping create a growing fuel shortage across Russia and is also harming the Kremlin's ability to finance the war. But European leaders fear that Trump's desperation to lower fuel prices ahead of next month's U.S. midterm elections by pressuring Kyiv to stop its attacks could weaken Ukraine’s hand without persuading Russia to end the war. Sybiha’s comments drew loud applause at the Warsaw conference and underscored growing tensions among Kyiv, Washington and Ukraine's European allies after Trump said the U.S. had agreed with Vladimir Putin to buy Russian diesel. The dispute between Washington and Kyiv overshadowed a Warsaw event that is normally strongly pro-American, given Poland's status as a key U.S. ally. "Ministers and heads of state won’t say so outright what they think about the Americans, but they certainly think a lot of things — the negotiations with Putin are yet another stab in the back for the Ukrainians," said a French lawmaker, speaking on condition of being granted anonymity. "You end the war by persuading the aggressor to limit his level of ambition, not by asking the victim to capitulate," said Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski. Advertisement Advertisement His German counterpart Johann Wadephul underlined that Berlin is pushing the Trump administration to fully impose energy sanctions approved by the U.S. Congress. On Sep. 18, Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Russia and Iran Sanctions Act of 2026, codifying existing US sanctions against Russia and expanding the scope for applying secondary sanctions, tariffs and restrictions, including against the energy sector. "This is not the time to lower the sanctions regime, but to strengthen it," Wadephul said. U.K. Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband echoed that call, saying Trump should exert pressure on Russia to agree to an energy ceasefire under which both warring nations would stop hitting each other's oil, gas, electricity and other assets. Russia has so far refused to take such a step. "Let us take seriously this issue of the energy ceasefire that President Trump has talked about, not simply a refinery ceasefire but a broad energy ceasefire, because in the last week alone we've seen 200 Russian attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure," Miliband said. Advertisement Advertisement Trump pressures Ukraine The U.S. president said on Monday that Putin is keener to end the fighting than Zelenskyy — despite the Kremlin not agreeing to any ceasefire. "I think actually Putin wants to make a deal more than Zelenskyy," Trump said. Since Trump announced an energy ceasefire — blindsiding both Kyiv and Moscow — Ukraine has paused bombing Russian refineries even as Russian attacks continue. While Trump wants the attacks to stop, Ukraine's European allies are keen to cripple Russia's war effort. "Ukraine is attacking refineries, which is having an effect, and data centers, which is also having an effect," Sikorski said. He also called on Poland's MAGA-aligned President Karol Nawrocki to use his influence with Trump "to explain to him that Putin is the aggressor and Zelenskyy is the victim of aggression." Wadephul added that he had talked to Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov during the U.N. General Assembly in New York last month, and saw no interest from him in ending the war. Advertisement Advertisement "A lot of people in Europe and especially in Germany were asking us and me, 'Why don't you talk to the Russians?' So now I had that conversation, and you saw the result," he said. "It's a very dire result. And it shows that Russia right now is not ready for ceasefire." During the same Warsaw event, Sybiha was forced to deny rumors that Washington may have stopped sharing intelligence with Kyiv in retaliation for its campaign of deep strikes against Russian oil refineries. "You are asking me if we are getting intelligence data from the American side. Yes, we continue this cooperation," he said. Concerns about a potential cut-off in U.S. intelligence grew on Tuesday after Ukraine's threat detection system failed to detect ballistic missiles that battered Kyiv overnight. Sybiha said the failure was due to a "special type of weaponry which was used by the Russian side." Zelenskyy also underlined the need for continued intelligence sharing. "There was also a rather treacherous ballistic missile strike on Kyiv — five missiles that hit civilian infrastructure. Unfortunately, there was no warning from our partners regarding this strike. Intelligence on Russian ballistic missile launches helps save lives." Sybiha stressed that Kyiv needs to continue strengthening its ability to fend off Russia's constant air attacks while Ukraine's troops push back against Russian forces on the front lines. Advertisement Advertisement "The future of Europe and the global security architecture is now being decided in Ukraine," he said. Chris Lunday and Laura Kayali contributed to this report.
